summary.title: Build Your Own Container Using Less than 100 Lines of Go
summary.one_liner: You learn how Linux containers are built from namespaces, cgroups and a pivot_root'ed root filesystem by writing a toy container runtime in under 100 lines of Go.
keywords: how does docker work under the hood
copy on write filesystem btrfs aufs
takeaways: Containers are built mainly from namespaces (isolation), cgroups (resource limits) and layered filesystems (efficient root filesystem images).
A minimal container can be made in Go by re-executing /proc/self/exe with the child argument and setting Cloneflags for UTS, PID and mount namespaces.
Swapping the root filesystem uses a bind mount of the rootfs onto itself followed by syscall.PivotRoot and chdir to /.
The article notes that the toy version skips cgroups, networking, uid switching and capability dropping, and is not for production use.
Containers are a technology rather than a user experience; PaaS platforms such as Cloud Foundry hide them behind code-based workflows.
summary.summary: The InfoQ article by Julian Friedman, an engineering lead on Cloud Foundry's Garden, explains what a container actually is by separating the analogy from the underlying Linux mechanisms. It describes six namespaces (PID, MNT, NET, UTS, IPC, USER), cgroups for resource sharing, and layered filesystems, using a simple copy for the root filesystem. It then walks through five code steps that build a basic Go program which re-runs itself, adds namespace flags, and pivot_roots into a rootfs. The author closes by arguing that containers are a technology to build developer experiences on, citing PaaS offerings as examples.
